algorithm.name: Top-K Streaming via Fixed-Size Min-Heap
algorithm.description: Maintain a binary min-heap of exactly K=100 elements keyed by item timestamp. For each of N incoming items: (1) push unconditionally while |H| < K; (2) if item.timestamp > heap.peek_min(), evict the minimum and push the new item; (3) otherwise discard the item in O(1). After all N items, the heap holds exactly the K items with the largest timestamps globally.

input.description: A one-pass stream of N=1,000,000 items, each carrying a comparable timestamp. Only O(K) working memory is permitted.
constraints: Items arrive in arbitrary, potentially adversarial timestamp order
Single-pass streaming: no random access or second pass available
Timestamps are totally ordered; O(1) comparison
input.dataStructure: Array-backed binary min-heap of capacity K

output.description: The K items with the globally largest timestamps among all N streamed items
properties: Every returned item's timestamp ≥ every discarded item's timestamp
Heap is unordered internally; if rank order is needed, sort the K-element result in O(K log K)

algorithm.pseudocode:
TOP-K-STREAM(stream, K):
  H ← new MinHeap(capacity=K)      // keyed by item.timestamp
  for each item x in stream:
    if |H| < K:
      MIN-HEAP-PUSH(H, x)           // O(log K) — fill phase
    else if x.timestamp > HEAP-MINIMUM(H):  // O(1) peek
      HEAP-EXTRACT-MIN(H)           // O(log K) — evict worst
      MIN-HEAP-PUSH(H, x)           // O(log K) — admit new
    // else: x.timestamp ≤ heap min → x cannot be in top-K; discard
  return H                          // K items with largest timestamps

CORRECTNESS (Loop Invariant):
  After processing items 1..i (i ≥ K), H contains exactly the K items
  with the largest timestamps among items 1..i.
  Init:   After K items, H holds all K — trivially correct.
  Maint:  If x.timestamp > H.min, x beats the weakest current member;
          evict it, admit x — invariant preserved.
          If x.timestamp ≤ H.min, x cannot displace any current member;
          discarding preserves invariant.
  Term:   After N items, H = top-K globally. □

timeComplexity.recurrence: Not recursive; iterative scan of N items, each costing at most 2 × O(log K) heap operations.

timeComplexity.amortized: Amortized O(log K) per item — each item triggers at most one push + one pop, each O(log K); fills (first K items) trigger only pushes.

concreteNumbers.speedupFactor: ≈ 1.5× fewer comparisons; ≈ 3× better if stream admits many early discards

spaceComplexity.auxiliary: O(K) — heap stores at most K items at any time; K=100 elements × ~64 bytes/item = ~6.4 KB, fitting in L1 cache
spaceComplexity.total: O(N + K) — input stream O(N) + heap O(K); for true streaming (items not buffered), effective footprint is O(K)

dataStructure.name: Binary Min-Heap (array-backed, fixed capacity K)
dataStructure.description: Standard binary heap stored in a length-K array. The minimum element (weakest timestamp) lives at index 0 and is the eviction candidate. All heap invariant operations are O(log K) on this fixed-size structure.

operations.name: peek-min
operations.description: Read heap[0] — the current smallest timestamp in the top-K set. Used to decide whether each incoming item qualifies.

operations.name: push (sift-up)
operations.description: Insert new item at end of array, swap upward while parent.timestamp > child.timestamp.

operations.name: extract-min (sift-down)
operations.description: Swap heap[0] with last element, shrink size, sift-down from root. Evicts the weakest current top-K member.

dataStructure.cacheNote: For K=100, the entire heap (~6.4 KB) fits in an L1 cache (typically 32–64 KB). Every sift-up/sift-down traverses at most log₂(100) ≈ 7 levels — all accesses hit cache, giving excellent practical performance despite the theoretical log factor.

alternatives.name: Full Sort + Slice (Merge Sort / Timsort)
alternatives.reason: Sorts all 1M items unconditionally, including the 999,900 items that will never appear in the output. Requires O(N) memory — 1M items cannot be streamed; entire dataset must be buffered. For K=100, N=1M: log N ≈ 20 vs. log K ≈ 7, roughly 3× more work. Streaming-incompatible.

alternatives.name: Randomized Quickselect (CLRS §9.2)
alternatives.reason: Finds the K-th order statistic in O(N) expected time — better asymptotically — but (a) requires all N items in memory simultaneously (streaming-incompatible); (b) returns a single pivot value, not the K items; finding all K items requires an additional O(K log K) sort pass; (c) O(N²) worst case without median-of-medians. Not usable here.

alternatives.name: Deterministic Linear Select / Introselect (CLRS §9.3)
alternatives.reason: Median-of-medians guarantees O(N) worst-case, eliminating Quickselect's adversarial risk. Still requires buffering all N items — streaming-incompatible. If the dataset fits in memory and K ≈ N/2, this would be preferred over the min-heap approach.

alternatives.name: Max-Heap Heapify + K Extractions (CLRS §6.3)
alternatives.reason: Floyd's linear-time bottom-up heapify builds a max-heap over all N items in O(N); K extract-max calls cost O(K log N) ≈ O(100 × 20) = O(2000) — effectively O(N) total. Asymptotically competitive but requires O(N) memory for the full heap. Optimal when data already resides in memory and K is large (K > N / log N ≈ 50,000 for N=1M).

alternatives.name: Order-Statistics Tree (Red-Black BST of size K)
alternatives.reason: Same O(N log K) asymptotic time and O(K) space as the min-heap, with the bonus of O(log K) rank queries. However, pointer-based BST nodes incur ~3–5× more memory per element and poor cache locality versus the contiguous array heap. No practical advantage for this problem; heap wins on constants.

alternatives.name: Reservoir Sampling (CLRS-adjacent: randomized streaming)
alternatives.reason: Produces a uniformly random sample of K items — not the top-K by timestamp. Incorrect for this problem. Mentioned to explicitly rule out a commonly confused algorithm.

comparison.justification: The min-heap is the uniquely correct choice given the three simultaneous constraints: (1) STREAMING — O(K) working memory, no full dataset buffering; (2) CORRECTNESS — greedy invariant provably produces the global top-K; (3) EFFICIENCY — O(N log K) ≈ O(6.64N) vs. O(N log N) ≈ O(19.93N), a concrete 3× comparison reduction for K=100, N=1M. The K=100-element heap (~6.4 KB) fits entirely in L1 cache, making the practical constant factor very small. No other algorithm satisfies all three constraints simultaneously.

assumptions: K=100 is known a priori and fixed for the lifetime of the stream
Item timestamps are totally ordered with a O(1) < comparator (integers, floats, epoch milliseconds)
Single-pass streaming model: items are consumed one at a time and cannot be revisited
Ties broken arbitrarily — no stable-selection requirement among equal timestamps
The output need not be sorted; if sorted rank order is required, add O(K log K) = O(664) final sort — negligible
N=1,000,000 is the total stream length; if N is unknown, the algorithm is self-terminating and correct at any stopping point
keyInsight: The heap minimum is a live threshold — 'the timestamp of the weakest item currently in the top-K' — so every new item is either accepted by beating this threshold (O(log K)) or rejected by falling below it (O(1)), meaning the full N-item dataset is never materialized and no comparison is wasted on elements that cannot affect the answer.
